newsitem.title: USA: US loan disclosure law reform not seen before 1998.
newsitem.headline: US loan disclosure law reform not seen before 1998.

text.p: Congress is unlikely to pass needed reform of two U.S. laws requiring disclosure on consumer loans until next year, legislators said Tuesday.
Enacted in the 1970s, the Truth in Lending Act and the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Acts were intended to deter deceptive sales practices and to help consumers comparison shop for loans.
But the mortgage market has changed significantly over the past 20 years and surveys now indicate most consumers are bewildered by the convoluted loan process.
"While no one finds fault with these objectives, in reality, these statutes are hurting consumers," Sen. Lauch Faircloth, a North Carolina Republican, said at a hearing to discuss reforming the laws.

Federal regulators are meeting with consumer and industry groups to try to come up with a reform proposal supported by all, said Faircloth, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee's financial institutions subcommittee.
"I look forward to seeing what the parties have agreed upon next year so that we can pass legislation to give consumers information and choices," he said.

Regulators at the hearing said one problem was the timing of disclosures. Consumer borrowers may not receive mandated disclosures about the cost of a loan until after they have paid a non-refundable application fee.
Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said the central bank, which writes rules to implement one of the laws, could not fix such problems on its own.

"The timing requirements are hard-coded into the statute and we cannot change that by regulation," Meyer said at the hearing. "Many of the other provisions that are at issue here are also hard-coded."

The Fed and the Department of Housing and Urban Development, which implements rules for the other law, are working on recommendations on how the laws could be rewritten, Meyer said. "Our goal is to provide recommendations to the Congress by the end of the year," he said.

Disclosure of fees paid to mortgage brokers, another controversial aspect of the laws, will be addressed in a proposed HUD rule expected later this summer, assistant Housing Secretary Nicholas Retsinas said.
Consumers who use a mortgage broker to secure a loan may not realize that the broker can be paid a fee by the lender.
Consumer groups charge that one type of undisclosed fee, called a "yield spread premium," is paid by lenders to brokers for convincing a borrower to pay a higher rate of interest.
In most states, the broker owes no legal duty to the borrower to find the best loan deal, although consumers often believe such a duty exists.

Dozens of lawsuits are pending alleging that the payment of yield spread premiums violates the Real Estate Settlement law. Some in the mortgage industry have asked Congress to impose a moratorium on the suits until the law is reformed, but few legislators voiced support for such a move.

At Tuesday's hearing, Retsinas declined to give HUD's position on the lawsuits. He said the current law would not allow HUD to ban such payments but added that a proposed rule to be issued in a few weeks would require enhanced disclosure of the fees.
Faircloth criticized the agency for failing to take a position. "HUD has simply let the consumer and the industry down," he said.
